extracted.intended_audience: agency staff, regulators, administrative lawyers, policy advocates, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative criteria about how agencies should treat, evaluate, and manage large volumes of public comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking, including the value of individual comments, processing challenges, and appropriate agency responses. Focuses on preserving public participation while ensuring comment integrity and usefulness to decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter false and bot comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must filter false and bot comments from their dockets and act to deter them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and remove comments attributed to people who did not submit them or to nonexistent people, and take measures to deter automated/bot submissions. This is a management and integrity priority distinct from discouraging genuine individual participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve access to individual comments (do not discourage mass comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not respond to large numbers of individual comments by discouraging genuine individual participation or treating rulemaking as a plebiscite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While mass comment events create management challenges, the open door to large volumes of comments 'cannot be closed, practically or legally.' Agencies should focus on management and integrity rather than deterrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the value of individual comments (views, experiences, data, arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments from individuals can be informational, supplying on-the-ground experiences, data, or arguments relevant to an agency’s decision; views and preferences are frequently relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA entitles 'interested persons' to submit 'written data, views, or arguments.' Even when comments express preferences rather than technical analysis, they often bear on value-laden policy choices (e.g., dignity, quality of life, community impacts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss comments solely because they use language suggested by groups
rubrics_metrics.description: That a comment uses language suggested by groups should not be a reason to dismiss it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-funded groups and companies often professionally draft comments; identical or similar wording does not necessarily negate an individual's genuine viewpoint. Evaluate the substantive content and context rather than form-letter similarity alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider disclosed commenter identity as context
rubrics_metrics.description: A commenter's identity, where disclosed, can provide important context to the decision-making agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details like lived experience (e.g., a prosthetic leg for ADA comments) or residence near polluting sources can materially inform the weight and relevance of a comment. Use disclosed identity to interpret perspective and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must consider comments expressing views (legal obligation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies cannot legally refuse to consider comments expressing views, even if they mainly focus on preferences rather than technical data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking is not a plebiscite, and agencies must weigh many statutory factors, but the APA's allowance for 'views' means such submissions must be considered rather than excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate publicly which comments will be most relevant and helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must continue to communicate openly about the comments that will be most relevant and helpful in a rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide guidance to the public on what kind of evidence, data, or arguments will assist the agency's analysis. Clear front-end communication can improve the signal-to-noise ratio of submissions and help commenters focus on useful content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat large comment volumes as signals worthy of engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: A large volume of individual comments dominated by views or preferences might tip an agency off to unnoticed or under-communicated perspectives, important pockets of public resistance, or widespread misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding might include pausing to engage affected communities, undertaking outreach, convening focus groups, or conducting additional analysis. Use volume as a prompt to assess whether further engagement or clarification is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address misinformation through public education and outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: When comments reveal public misunderstanding or misinformation, agencies should consider responding with public education rather than simply acquiescing to misguided preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: convene focus groups and run information campaigns to correct misconceptions (e.g., Clinton DOT airbag rule example). Public education can improve public understanding and better ensure policy goals like safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and answer comments, even briefly
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency should acknowledge and answer comments, even briefly, to convey that individuals expressing views have been heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief responses in rulemaking records (e.g., DoD response to sexual assault prevention comments, FCC net neutrality responses) help legitimacy and democratic responsiveness even when the agency ultimately gives greater weight to other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh public views against statutory and technical factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may determine in particular cases that public views should yield to other statutory or technical factors; public preference is one input among many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the legal constraint that agencies must consider numerous statutory factors beyond public preferences. Treat comments as informative but not dispositive; document reasons when other considerations prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on management challenges to ensure comment integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than discouraging genuine commenters, agencies should focus on the operational and managerial challenges of processing very large comment volumes while ensuring integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop systems and practices to sort, screen, and analyze massive comment datasets; distinguish bots/fraud from genuine submissions; and preserve the democratic potential of public participation.
